title: Sunset Point to Sunrise Point
subtitle: Bryce Canyon National Park
description: A big Bryce view without a big climb: follow the paved rim between Sunset and Sunrise Points and watch a whole amphitheater of hoodoos unfold below. Pause often, look for changing colors, and enjoy the kind of scenery that makes a first hike feel like an occasion. This guide covers only the short paved segment, not the full Rim Trail or a descent into the canyon.
difficulty: Easy (NPS); high elevation and winter ice change the demands
trailhead: Sunset Point or Sunrise Point parking area, Bryce Canyon National Park
preparation: Bring water, sun protection, layers, and shoes with grip. Remain on the paved rim segment for this outing; the full Rim Trail and routes descending below the rim have different demands.
hazards: Rim viewpoints have steep drop-offs. Stay behind barriers and keep young hikers close. Snow and ice can make paved surfaces hazardous; NPS recommends winter traction devices. Do not treat an easy summer rating as a winter safety assessment.

title: Jenny’s Canyon
subtitle: Snow Canyon State Park
description: A small adventure with a dramatic reveal: a sandy approach leads to a sculpted slot in Snow Canyon’s sandstone cliffs. Look closely at the wind-carved pockets and textures, or take the signed option toward the overlook if it suits your group. There is plenty to notice without needing a long day on the trail.
trailhead: Signed Jenny’s Canyon Trailhead in Snow Canyon State Park
preparation: Wear shoes that grip uneven rock and are comfortable in deep sand. Bring water and sun protection even for this short outing. Follow the marked trail across the dry wash and choose the slot or overlook branch according to your group’s comfort.
hazards: Deep sand and uneven rock can slow a group. A short canyon is still a place to avoid during storms or when flooding is possible; check official weather and park advice before entering. Extreme desert heat can overwhelm young hikers quickly.

title: Ladyfinger Point
subtitle: Antelope Island State Park
description: Meet a different side of Utah: island scenery, open skies, and a short route toward Ladyfinger Point. The small distance makes room to slow down, notice the Great Salt Lake landscape, and enjoy being outdoors together. Keep wildlife encounters at a respectful distance and let the views be the reward.
difficulty: First Steps editorial selection; official route-specific difficulty not located
trailhead: Ladyfinger Point trail at the north end of Antelope Island; use the official trail map to locate parking and the trail
preparation: Bring water, sun protection, and layers for changing conditions. Check the official map before leaving your vehicle. Allow extra time for views, wildlife, and any trail conditions that slow your group.
hazards: Give free-ranging bison and other wildlife ample space; never approach or disturb them. Biting midges can be a problem in spring (the park identifies April–June); ordinary repellent is ineffective against these gnats, and fine-mesh head nets are recommended. Mosquitoes can also be present in warmer months.

title: Sand Dune Arch
subtitle: Arches National Park
description: Follow a sandy passage between tall sandstone fins to find an arch tucked out of sight. The short approach feels like discovering a little outdoor room, with textures and shapes worth lingering over. This guide covers Sand Dune Arch and back only; continuing to Broken Arch makes a different, longer outing.
difficulty: Easy (NPS), with deep sand and a narrow passage
trailhead: Sand Dune Arch parking area, Arches National Park
preparation: Wear shoes suited to deep sand and rock. Bring water even for a short walk, and turn back if the narrow passage or sandy footing does not suit your group. The route is not wheelchair accessible according to NPS.
hazards: Do not climb or jump from the arch. Deep sand, rock, and the narrow passage can be awkward. Summer heat and sun exposure, sudden storms, and winter snow/ice can change the outing substantially.

title: Sunset Point
subtitle: Capitol Reef National Park
description: Watch the Waterpocket Fold’s cliffs change color as the light softens. This short walk offers a wide-open panorama and a reason to pause together, whether you visit in daylight or plan carefully for sunset. Bring a headlamp if you stay late: the return is part of the adventure too.
trailhead: End of the dirt Panorama Point Road, about one mile from the highway turnoff at Panorama Point; consult the official NPS route information
preparation: Bring water, sun protection, and a map. If visiting for sunset, allow time to walk both directions, pack layers, and carry a headlamp rather than relying only on a phone light.
hazards: Uneven ground and fading light can make the return harder. The park warns about intense summer sun, monsoon storms, and flash floods. Winter ice, snow, and cold can change a short trail’s demands; check conditions before choosing it.

title: Bridal Veil Falls
subtitle: Provo Canyon
description: Make a waterfall the reason for a first walk outdoors. Bridal Veil Falls pairs Provo Canyon scenery with paved riverside trails and nearby picnic areas. This guide covers the paved viewing approach only, not a climb beside or above the falls. Confirm the available pedestrian route and parking with Utah County before choosing this outing; construction access remains unverified.
difficulty: First Steps editorial selection for the paved viewing approach; official route-specific difficulty not published in reviewed sources
trailhead: Bridal Veil Falls main parking area, Provo Canyon off US Highway 189; confirm the currently authorized parking and pedestrian approach with Utah County.
preparation: Confirm parking, construction restrictions, and the available paved route with Utah County before leaving. Bring water, shoes with grip, and layers. Stay on the authorized viewing approach and respect barriers; this guide excludes climbing beside or above the waterfall.
hazards: Utah State Parks warns that snow can limit winter access. As conservative planning precautions, watch for wet or icy footing, keep children close beside the river, and avoid climbing wet rocks. Respect construction barriers and turn back if the authorized route is unclear.

title: Huber Grove Trail
subtitle: Wasatch Mountain State Park
description: Let your first outdoor adventures include a little history. Huber Grove brings together a self-guided nature trail, an aspen grove, an old orchard, and the story of early life in the Heber Valley. Take your time noticing the landscape and historic setting rather than treating the walk as a race.

trailhead: Visitor Center trail network, Wasatch Mountain State Park, Midway; confirm the Huber Grove route with visitor center staff
preparation: Stop at the visitor center to confirm the exact route, distance, footing, and return time before starting. Bring water, comfortable walking shoes, and layers. Stay on marked routes and respect historic structures and orchard rules.
hazards: Route-specific hazards and surface accessibility have not been fully documented in the reviewed official sources. Plan conservatively around wet or muddy footing, cold, snow, and ice; ask staff whether conditions suit your group.
